 right
 dorsolateral
 prefrontal
 cortex
 and
 bilateral
 inferior
 pari-
etal
 lobules
 [12].
 There
 was
 no
 neural
 overlap
 between
 late
 learning
and
 SWM.
 Thus
 we
 found
 that
 early
 but
 not
 late
 learning
 engages
SWM
 processes
 in
 young
 adults,
 compatible
 with
 other
 work
 docu-
menting
 greater
 cognitive
 demands
 during
 early
 learning
 [13–15].
In
 contrast,
 in
 a
 companion
 study
 we
 found
 that
 older
 adults
 (18
participants,
 71.4
 ±
 4.2
 years
 old)
 had
 a
 signiﬁcantly
 reduced
 rate
of
 early
 but
 not
 late
 learning
 in
 comparison
 to
 young
 adults
 (18
participants,
 21.1
 ±
 2.5
 years
 old
 [16]).
 Measures
 of
 working
 mem-
ory
 did
 not
 correlate
 with
 either
 the
 early
 or
 late
 learning
 period
for
 older
 adults.
 In
 addition,
 although
 older
 adults
 recruited
 the
right
 dorsolateral
 prefrontal
 cortex
 and
 bilateral
 inferior
 parietal
lobules
 in
 a
 comparable
 fashion
 to
 young
 adults
 during
 the
 SWM
task,
 they
 did
 not
 engage
 these
 regions
 during
 either
 early
 or
 late
learning.
 These
 ﬁndings
 suggest
 that
 older
 adults
 do
 not
 effectively
recruit
 available
 SWM
 resources
 to
 support
 early
 motor
 learning
processes.
The
 purpose
 of
 the
 current
 study
 is
 to
 investigate
 the
 contri-
bution
 of
 SWM
 to
 motor
 transfer
 for
 young
 and
 older
 adults.
 It
may
 be
 that
 older
 adults
 do
 not
 experience
 difﬁculties
 at
 trans-
fer
 of
 learning
 [8–10]
 because
 performance
 at
 transfer
 does
 not
require
 SWM
 engagement.
 Therefore,
 we
 hypothesize
 that
 SWM
performance
 measures
 will
 be
 less
 correlated
 with
 motor
 transfer
than
 with
 motor
 learning
 for
 both
 age
 groups.
 Further,
 we hypoth-
esize
 that
 both
 age
 groups
 will
 show
 reduced
 activation
 of
 brain
regions
 that
 contribute
 to
 SWM
 such
 as
 prefrontal
 and
 parietal
cortex
 at
 transfer
 of
 adaptation
 versus
 learning.
 Determining
 the
mechanisms
 underlying
 conditions
 in
 which
 older
 adults
 exhibit
preserved
 performance
 is
 an
 important
 ﬁrst
 step
 towards
 designing
targeted
 interventions
 to
 improve
 motor
 performance.
2.
 Material
 and
 methods
 Participants
 and
 procedure
2.1.
 (N
 =
 18,
 20.8
 ±
 2.5
 years
 old,
 14.6
 ±
 2.0
 years
 education,
 10
 female)
 and
older
Young
 adults
 (N
 =
 18,
 72.3
 ±
 4.7
 years
 old,
 15.9
 ±
 2.5
 years
 education,
 12
 female)
 were
recruited
 from
 the
 University
 of
 Michigan
 (UM)
 community
 and
 through
 the
 UM
 NIH
Claude
 D.
 Pepper
 Older
 American’s
 Independence
 Center
 human
 subjects
 and
 assess-
ment
 core.
 All
 participants
 signed
 an
 Internal
 Review
 Board
 (IRB)
 approved
 consent
form
 prior
 to
 entrance
 into
 the
 study.
 Participants
 were
 right
 handed
 (Edinburgh
Handedness
 Inventory
 [17], mean
 handedness
 scores:
 young
 adults
 88.6
 ±
 11.4,
older
 adults
 80.4
 ±
 13.8),
 free
 of
 contraindications
 for
 an
 fMRI
 study
 and
 scored
 a
minimum
 of
 26/30
 on
 the
 Mini
 Mental
 State
 Exam
 [18]
 and
 a
 minimum
 of
 123/144
on
 the
 Mattis
 Dementia
 Rating
 Scale
 [19].
 These
 participants
 were
 separate
 cohorts
from
 those
 that
 participated
 in
 similar
 experiments
 in
 the
 laboratory
 [10,12,16].
On
 day
 one
 of
 testing
 cognitive
 abilities
 were
 assessed
 through
 a
 battery
 of
 neu-
ropsychological
 tests.
 Spatial
 working
 memory
 was
 assessed
 with
 Thurston’s
 card
rotation
 task
 [20]
 and
 forward
 and
 backward
 Corsi
 Block
 tapping
 tests
 [21]. A
 brief
description
 of
 these
 tests
 appears
 in
 Table
 1.
 Following
 this,
 participants
 practiced
the
 baseline
 condition
 for
 the
 visuomotor
 adaptation
 task
 and
 the
 control
 condi-
tion
 for
 the
 spatial
 working
 memory
 task
 in
 a mock
 MRI
 scanner
 to
 become
 familiar
with
 the
 MRI
 environment
 and
 the
 experimental
 protocols.
 For
 the
 adaptation
 task,
participants
 moved
 a
 joystick
 with
 the
 dominant
 hand,
 and
 real-time
 feedback
 was
presented
 as
 a
 cursor
 moving
 on
 the
 display
 screen.
 The
 starting
 position
 of
 the
 cur-

Brief
 description
 of
 spatial
 working
 memory
 assessments
 and
 measurement
 units.

assessment

 unit

 two

 then
 state
 if
 the

 has
 been

 being
 turned

Number
 block

The
 experimenter
 taps
 a
sequence
 of
 correct
trials
Corsi
 of
 blocks
 and
 the
participant
 must
 reproduce
 the
sequence
 either
 in
 the
 same
order
 (forward)
 or
 reverse
order
 (backward)
sor
 for
 a given
 trial
 was
 the
 center
 of
 the
 screen.
 Targets
 would
 appear
 randomly
above,
 below,
 right
 or
 left
 of
 the
 original
 cursor
 position.
 Participants
 were
 instructed
to
 move
 the
 cursor
 as
 quickly
 and
 accurately
 as
 possible
 to
 the
 target,
 hold
 the
 cursor
in
 the
 target
 until
 the
 target
 disappeared
 and
 then
 release
 the
 spring-loaded
 joystick
allowing
 the
 cursor
 to
 return
 to
 the
 original
 centered
 position.
 A
 trial
 was
 deﬁned
as
 the
 time
 between
 the
 appearance
 and
 disappearance
 of
 the
 target
 (2.5
 s).
 In
 a
single
 run
 participants
 were
 given
 two
 blocks
 of
 12
 trials
 (20
 s
 visual
 ﬁxation,
 block
of
 12
 trials,
 20
 s visual
 ﬁxation,
 block
 of
 12
 trials,
 22
 s
 visual
 ﬁxation).
 Participants
practiced
 three
 runs
 of
 the
 task
 in
 the
 mock
 scanner.
In
 the
 spatial
 control
 task
 participants
 were
 presented
 with
 three
 closed
 circles
on
 the
 screen
 for
 500
 ms.
 Following
 a
 brief
 retention
 interval
 of
 250
 ms,
 an
 open
circle
 would
 appear.
 Participants
 responded
 with
 a
 button
 box,
 pressing
 the
 index
ﬁnger
 if
 the
 open
 circle
 was
 in
 the
 same
 location
 as
 one
 of
 the
 closed
 circles
 and
pressing
 the
 middle
 ﬁnger
 if
 the
 circle
 was
 in
 a
 different
 location.
 The
 open
 circle
was
 presented
 for
 2500
 ms followed
 by
 a ﬁxation
 screen
 for
 500
 ms
 and
 a
 blank
screen
 for
 another
 500
 ms.
 Participants
 practiced
 one
 block
 of
 10
 trials
 of
 the
 spatial
control
 task
 in
 the
 mock
 scanner.
The
 second
 day
 of
 testing
 was
 conducted
 at
 the
 UM
 Functional
 MRI
 Laboratory.
 A
series
 of
 scans
 were
 performed
 using
 a
 3.0
 T MRI
 scanner
 (General
 Electric,
 Wauke-
sha,
 WI).
 Participants’
 heads
 were
 comfortably
 restrained
 to
 reduce
 head
 movement.
They
 wore
 fMRI
 compatible
 mirrored
 goggles
 to
 view
 a
 screen
 for
 the
 visual
 stimuli.
Participants
 completed
 17
 runs
 of
 the
 joystick
 task
 during
 scanning.
 Some
 of
 the
runs
 included
 visual
 rotation
 of
 online
 feedback
 requiring
 visuomotor
 adaptation
to
 reach
 the
 target
 (supplemental
 materials
 Table
 S1). Three
 rotation
 magnitudes,
15◦, 30◦and
 45◦clockwise
 rotations
 of
 the
 feedback
 display
 about
 the
 center
 of
 the
screen,
 were
 presented
 to
 participants.
 Each
 magnitude
 of
 visual
 rotation
 was
 given
for
 three
 consecutive
 runs.
 Following
 each
 magnitude
 of
 visual
 rotation
 the
 display
returned
 to
 baseline
 conditions
 for
 two
 consecutive
 runs
 for
 washout
 of
 the
 adap-
tation
 (cf.
 [10,11]).
 Participants
 were
 presented
 the
 visual
 rotations
 in
 one
 of
 two
orders.
 Presentation
 order
 1
 (9
 young
 adults
 and
 9
 older
 adults)
 received
 the
 visual
rotations
 in
 the
 order
 of
 30◦, 15◦and
 45◦. Presentation
 order
 2
 (a
 separate
 group
 of
9
 young
 adults
 and
 9
 older
 adults)
 received
 the
 visual
 rotations
 in
 the
 order
 of
 45◦,
15◦and
 30◦. Using
 two
 presentation
 orders
 allowed
 us
 to
 compare
 participants
 that
received
 the
 30◦rotation
 ﬁrst
 (order
 1)
 to
 participants
 that
 received
 the
 30◦rotation
last
 (order
 2)
 and
 likewise
 for
 the
 45◦rotation.
Following
 the
 visuomotor
 adaptation
 task
 participants
 were
 presented
 with
 the
same
 spatial
 control
 task
 that
 they
 practiced
 in
 the
 mock
 scanner.
 In
 a
 single
 run,
participants
 were
 given
 four
 blocks
 of
 10
 trials
 interspersed
 with
 20
 s
 visual
 ﬁxation
periods.
 Eighty
 percent
 of
 the
 trials
 were
 ‘match’
 trials
 in
 the
 control
 task.
 Partic-
ipants
 were
 also
 given
 a
 SWM
 task
 in
 the
 scanner,
 (similar
 to
 those
 used
 in
 refs.
[12,22]).
 Three
 closed
 circles
 appeared
 on
 the
 screen
 for
 500
 m. After
 the
 3
 s reten-
tion
 interval
 the
 probe
 set
 was
 presented
 on
 the
 screen
 for
 3000
 ms.
 Participants
responded
 with
 the
 index
 ﬁnger
 using
 the
 button
 box
 if
 the
 target
 and
 probe
 set
 were
in
 the
 same
 conﬁguration,
 but
 rotated
 (match).
 If
 the
 conﬁguration
 was
 different,
participants
 pressed
 the
 middle
 ﬁnger
 (non
 match).
 Participants
 performed
 three
runs
 of
 this
 task
 (two
 blocks
 of
 10
 trials
 separated
 by
 20
 s
 visual
 ﬁxation
 periods).
Seventy
 percent
 of
 the
 trials
 were
 ‘match’
 trials.
 A
 single-shot
 gradient-echo
 reverse
spiral
 pulse
 sequence
 was
 also
 used
 to
 acquire
 the
 fMRI
 data.
 Pulse
 sequence
 param-
eters
 were
 TR/TE/FA/FOV
 of
 2000
 ms/30
 ms/80/220
 mm respectively.
 Forty,
 3.2
 mm
thick
 slightly
 oblique
 axial
 slices
 (no
 gap)
 were
 acquired.
 High
 resolution
 anatomical
images
 were
 also
 acquired
 using
 a
 T1-weighted
 gradient-echo
 pulse
 sequence
 with
the
 following
 parameters
 TR/TE/FA/FOV
 200
 ms/3.7
 ms/90/220
 mm and
 a
 voxel
 size
of
 1
 mm ×
 1
 mm ×
 1.2
 mm.
 Behavioral
 data
 analysis
2.2.
 Labview
 6.1
 software
 (National
 Instruments)
 was
 used
 to
 analyze
 the
joystick
Custom
 data
 ofﬂine.
 A
 dual
 pass
 Butterworth
 digital
 ﬁlter
 [23]
 using
 a cutoff
 fre-
quency
 of
 10
 Hz
 was
 used
 to
 ﬁlter
 the
 raw
 data.
 The
 resultant
 joystick
 path
 was
calculated
 by
 computing
 the
 square
 root
 of
 the
 sum
 of
 the
 squared
 X and
 Y coor-
dinate
 data
 at
 each
 time
 point.
 The
 tangential
 velocity
 proﬁle
 was
 then
 calculated
through
 differentiation.
 The
 optimal
 algorithm
 of
 Teasdale
 et
 al.
 [24]
 was
 used
 to
determine
 movement
 onset
 and
 offset.
 Performance
 on
 the
 task
 was
 measured
 by
reaction
 time
 (RT),
 direction
 error
 (DE)
 and
 initial
 endpoint
 error
 (IEE).
 RT
 was
 com-
puted
 by
 subtracting
 the
 time
 of
 the
 stimulus
 presentation
 from
 the
 time
 of
 the
onset
 of
 movement.
 DE
 is
 determined
 by
 the
 angle
 between
 a
 direct
 line
 to
 the
target
 and
 the
 spatial
 position
 of
 the
 cursor
 at
 peak
 velocity.
 IEE
 represents
 the
 dis-
tance
 from
 the
 joystick
 controlled
 cursor
 and
 the
 target
 at
 the
 end
 of
 the
 ﬁrst
 ballistic
movement.
 The
 algorithm
 used
 to
 calculate
 IEE
 identiﬁes
 a
 period
 of
 acceleration
following
 a
 period
 of
 deceleration
 or
 a change
 in
 the
 sign
 of
 the
 velocity.
 These
 vari-
ables
 were
 calculated
 for
 each
 trial.
 To
 assess
 rate
 of
 change
 in
 performance,
 the
slopes
 of
 DE
 across
 initial
 learning
 trials
 (run
 3)
 and
 motor
 transfer
 trials
 (run
 13)
were
 determined.
 For
 both
 the
 spatial
 control
 task
 and
 the
 SWM
 task
 the
 average
percent
 accuracy
 and
 RT
 for
 the
 run
 was
 calculated.
The
 amount
 of
 learning
 that
 occurred
 during
 the
 ﬁrst
 experience
 with
 the
 visuo-
motor
 adaptation
 task
 was
 quantiﬁed
 since
 total
 learning
 may
 impact
 the
 amount
of
 transfer.
 We computed
 the
 amount
 of
 learning
 as
 the
 amount
 of
 actual
 correction
that
 occurred
 as
 a
 percentage
 of
 the
 magnitude
 of
 correction
 necessary
 to
 return
to
 baseline.
 The
 mean
 of
 run
 13
 (initial
 transfer)
 was
 divided
 by
 the
 mean
 of
 run
 3
(initial
 learning).
 A
 score
 below
 1
 would
 represent
 that
 learning
 during
 the
 ﬁrst
